Book-and-claim decouples the physical location of where SAF is used from its environmental value. The Massachusetts Institute of Technology’s Center for Transportation & Logistics in partnership with the Smart Freight Centre developed guidelines to enable book-and-claim (Massachusetts Institute of Technology 2021). The “book” refers to SAF producers’ generation of certificates (also referred to as credits) documenting a volume of SAF that was produced and consumed. The “claim” refers to the purchasers of certificates such as airlines or corporations who claim the emissions reductions. SAF qualifies as an advanced biofuel under the Renewable Fuel Standard, and obligated parties must meet volume requirements. There are values attached to the renewable identification number system used to track compliance. States have introduced various mechanisms to enable SAF markets. SAF qualifies for tradeable credit values in states with Low Carbon Fuel Standards, including California, New Mexico, Oregon, and Washington. The following states provide SAF-specific incentives: • Illinois: $1.50/gallon for SAF purchased or used in the state by airline common carriers effective through Dec. 31, 2032 (Illinois Department of Revenue 2023). • Minnesota: $1.50/gallon for SAF produced or blended in the state and used for flights departing Minnesota effective through July 1, 2030. There is also a sales exemption for SAF facility construction materials through July 1, 2034 (Minnesota Department of Revenue 2025). • Nebraska: $0.75/gallon (up to an additional $0.50/gallon for emissions reductions exceeding 50%) effective through Jan. 1, 2035 (Nebraska Farm Bureau 2024). • Washington: The following incentive is triggered if in-state SAF production reaches 20 million gallons/year and is effective for 10 years (Port of Seattle 2023): $1.00/gallon (up to $2.00/gallon for emissions reductions exceeding 50%) for SAF produced or blended in-state for flights departing Washington. 1.4 E-Fuel SAF Technology PtL is an emerging technology where electricity and/or low-carbon hydrogen is used to convert CO into intermediate products such as syngas or alcohols (Figure 4). These intermediate 2 products can be converted to SAF using ASTM-approved pathways including FT to convert syngas to SAF and ATJ converting methanol or other intermediate alcohols to SAF. The motivation for SAF via PtL technology is the potential to significantly reduce emissions by using CO as a feedstock. For PtL to find success in the marketplace, a plant needs access to low-cost 2 and low-carbon electricity, a reliable source of CO , and a source of low-carbon hydrogen. 2 Research is focused on electrolyzers—devices that split water into hydrogen and oxygen. Electrolyzer research is focused on reducing capital costs, improving efficiency, and increasing the useful life to greater than 70,000 hours.
